definition: Native-language identification (NLI) is the task of determining an author's native language (L1) based only on their writings in a second language (L2).
details: NLI works through identifying language-usage patterns that are common to specific L1 groups and then applying this knowledge to predict the native language of previously unseen texts. This is motivated in part by applications in second-language acquisition, language teaching and forensic linguistics, amongst others.

explainer.lead: NLI predicts an author's native language from how they write in a second language. It matters for second-language acquisition, language teaching and forensic linguistics.

tiers.eli5: By spotting the habits someone carries into a second language, you can guess which language they grew up speaking.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers learn language-usage patterns shared by specific L1 groups and apply them to unseen L2 texts. A pitfall is that patterns common to one L1 group may be confounded with other author traits.
tiers.paperLevel: Task: given text written in L2, predict the author's L1. It relies on identifying usage patterns common to specific L1 groups and generalizing them to new texts; accuracy depends on how distinctive those patterns are.

explainer.example: From an essay written in English, the system infers the writer's native language by matching patterns typical of a particular L1 group.
